title: Surfing: Riding the Waves
summary: How wind forms ocean waves, how a board's buoyancy and balance let a surfer catch and ride them, and how surfers read wave patterns to find the best wave.
poll: Reading the ocean well is just as important to surfing as standing on the board.

versions.title: Riding Waves
versions.text:
Paddle out. Catch a wave. Stand up. This is surfing!

Wind blows over the ocean. It pushes the water. This makes a wave.

A surfer lies on a board. The board floats on top of the water. The surfer paddles with both arms.

When a wave comes near, the surfer paddles fast. This can match the speed of the wave. Then the wave can pick up the board.

The surfer jumps up to stand. She bends her knees low. This helps her stay up on the board.

Near the shore, the water gets less deep. The bottom of the wave slows down. The top of the wave still moves fast. So the wave gets tall, and then it breaks.

A good surfer watches the waves. She looks for the best wave to ride.

Surfing takes balance and practice. It is fun to ride a wave all the way in.

Paddling out, catching a wave, and standing up: surfing combines these three actions into one continuously exciting ocean sport.

A surfer lies flat on a board, which floats because of buoyancy: the board displaces some water, and that water pushes back up with a force equal to the weight displaced. The surfer paddles steadily with both arms, trying to match the exact speed of an oncoming wave.

As a chosen wave approaches, the surfer paddles hard to match its speed precisely. Once the two speeds match, the sloped face of the wave catches the board and lets it glide forward under its own momentum, much like sliding down a gentle, moving hill.

The surfer then pushes up to stand, bending the knees low and keeping the body's weight centered directly over the board. This careful balance lets the surfer steer along the open face of the wave, safely away from its breaking crest.

Close to shore, the ocean becomes shallow, and the base of the wave slows noticeably because of friction with the sea floor, while the top of the wave keeps racing ahead at its original speed. This difference in speed makes the wave steepen until its crest curls over and finally breaks.

Surfers also study ocean currents carefully, since a strong current can quietly pull a board away from the best part of an approaching wave.

Surfing takes balance, careful timing, and years of practice, and it feels wonderful to glide smoothly all the way to the shore.

questions.stem: How is the article mainly organized?
options: As a timeline of one surfer's first wave
By explaining swells, buoyancy, glide, and waves
As a comparison between surfing and sailing
As instructions for building a surfboard
questions.why: Each part of the article explains a different piece of surfing, from how swells form to how waves break.

wrong.A: No single surfer's story is told from start to finish.
wrong.C: Sailing is not compared to surfing.
wrong.D: Building a surfboard is not explained.

questions.stem: Based on the article, how is a swell different from the moment a wave breaks?
options: A swell is waves far out; breaking is near shore
A swell and a breaking wave are the same thing
A swell happens only at night, waves break by day
A swell is caused by surfers, breaking by the wind
questions.why: The article describes a swell as waves moving across deep water, while breaking happens later, near the shore, when the crest curls over.

wrong.B: The article treats these as two different stages, not the same thing.
wrong.C: Time of day is not connected to swells or breaking in the article.
wrong.D: Wind, not surfers, forms a swell, and friction near shore causes breaking.

MID.prompt: Imagine you are explaining surfing to a beginner. Describe how a swell becomes a wave a surfer can ride, using at least two key words from the article.
checklist: I explained how a swell travels toward the shore.
I explained how a surfer catches and rides the wave.
I used at least two key words correctly.
MID.modelAnswer: A swell is a group of waves moving together across deep water, and as it nears the shore, the surfer's board floats because of buoyancy while she paddles to match the wave's speed. Once the speeds match, she stands and glides along the open face of the wave, steering away from the crest and watching for any current that might pull her off course.

keyWords.definition: the force an object has because it is moving, which depends on its speed and mass
keyWords.example: The sled gained momentum as it raced down the snowy slope.

keyWords.definition: the force that pulls objects toward the Earth
keyWords.example: Gravity pulls a dropped apple straight down to the ground.

keyWords.definition: a force that slows an object when it rubs against another surface
keyWords.example: Friction between the tires and the road helps a bicycle stop.

keyWords.definition: the curved path an object follows as it moves
keyWords.example: The ball's trajectory arced high over the fence.

keyWords.definition: to guess what will happen next and get ready for it
keyWords.example: A soccer goalkeeper must anticipate which way a shot will go.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Surfing results depend almost entirely on luck
A surfer's glide and timing rely on gravity and momentum
Physics explains sailing better than it explains surfing
Only board size determines how a wave is ridden
questions.why: The article connects buoyancy, gravity, momentum, friction, and anticipation to how a surfer catches and rides a wave.

wrong.A: The article credits timing and physics, not luck.
wrong.C: The article applies physics to surfing specifically, not sailing.
wrong.D: Timing and balance matter at least as much as board size.

questions.stem: According to the article, what happens to the board once gravity pulls it down the sloped face of a wave?
options: It loses all of its momentum almost instantly
It stops moving until the surfer paddles again
It gains momentum along a curving trajectory forward
It sinks straight down to the ocean floor
questions.why: In the article, gravity gives the board momentum that carries it forward along a curving trajectory.

wrong.A: Momentum builds, according to the article, rather than disappearing.
wrong.B: The board keeps moving on its own at this point.
wrong.D: The board glides along the wave's face, not down to the floor.

questions.stem: According to the article, how do skilled surfers anticipate where a wave will break?
options: By reading how the wave rises and curls
By asking a lifeguard to point out the spot
By waiting for another surfer to catch it first
By measuring the water's temperature
questions.why: In the article, surfers anticipate the break point by reading how the wave rises and curls.

wrong.B: Lifeguards are not described as pointing out breaks.
wrong.C: Waiting for another surfer is not the method described.
wrong.D: Water temperature is not connected to anticipating a break.

questions.stem: Why does friction with the sea floor cause a wave to steepen near the shore?
options: Friction speeds up the top of the wave even more
Friction pushes the whole wave sideways
Friction causes the wind to stop blowing
Friction slows the base while the top races ahead
questions.why: In the article, friction slows the wave's base while the top keeps racing ahead, which steepens the wave.

wrong.A: Friction slows, rather than speeds up, part of the wave.
wrong.B: Sideways movement is not described as an effect of friction.
wrong.C: Wind is not affected by friction with the sea floor.

questions.stem: A surfer fails to anticipate when a wave will break and paddles into position too late. Based on the article, what is the most likely result?
options: The wave will wait for her to catch up
Her board will automatically gain extra buoyancy
She is more likely to miss the best part of the wave
The current will carry her closer to the crest
questions.why: Since anticipation helps a surfer paddle into position at the right moment, reacting too late makes missing the best part of the wave more likely.

wrong.A: Waves do not wait for a surfer to catch up.
wrong.B: Timing does not change a board's buoyancy.
wrong.D: A current pulling toward the crest is not described as a benefit of poor timing.

questions.stem: Based on the article, how does gravity's role in surfing differ from friction's role?
options: Gravity and friction both speed up the board equally on every wave
Gravity pulls the board forward; friction slows the wave's base
Gravity only matters near shore, and friction only matters far from it
Neither gravity nor friction affects a surfer's ride on the water
questions.why: Gravity pulls the board down the wave's face to generate momentum, while friction with the sea floor slows the wave's base near the shore.

wrong.A: Friction slows rather than speeds up the wave's base.
wrong.C: The article describes gravity acting on the wave's face generally, not only near shore.
wrong.D: Both forces are described as affecting the ride.

questions.stem: The article says a board follows a curving trajectory. What does trajectory mean here?
options: The path the board follows as it moves
The exact weight of the surfboard
A rule enforced by ocean lifeguards
The sound a wave makes as it breaks
questions.why: Trajectory refers to the curved path the board follows as momentum carries it forward.

wrong.B: Trajectory describes a path, not a weight.
wrong.C: Trajectory is not a lifeguard rule.
wrong.D: Trajectory does not refer to sound.

questions.stem: Why does the author explain the physics behind catching and riding a wave in such detail?
options: To argue that only scientists can enjoy surfing
To convince readers surfing is more dangerous than other sports
To compare surfing unfavorably with sailing
To show a surfer's choices depend on real physical forces
questions.why: By explaining buoyancy, gravity, momentum, friction, and anticipation, the author shows that a surfer's split-second choices have a physical explanation.

wrong.A: The explanation is written for general readers, not only scientists.
wrong.B: Danger compared to other sports is not discussed.
wrong.C: Sailing is not compared in this article.

HIGH.prompt: Choose two physical forces or ideas from the article and explain how each helps a surfer catch or ride a wave.
checklist: I explained one physical force or idea and connected it to catching or riding a wave.
I explained a second physical force or idea and connected it to catching or riding a wave.
I used precise vocabulary, including at least two key words.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Buoyancy keeps a surfer's board floating on the water, which lets her paddle out and match the speed of an oncoming wave. Once she catches the wave, gravity pulls the board down its sloped face, building momentum that carries it forward along a smooth trajectory, while friction with the sea floor near the shore makes the wave steepen and finally break, so a surfer must anticipate that moment to ride the wave well.

LOW.stem: What does a surfer use to paddle?
options: A small oar
Her feet
Both arms
A long rope
LOW.why: The text says the surfer paddles with both arms.

wrong.A: The text does not say a surfer uses an oar.
wrong.B: The surfer lies on the board and uses her arms, not her feet.
wrong.D: A rope is not mentioned for paddling.

LOW.stem: Why does a good surfer watch the waves?
options: To find the best wave to ride
To count how many waves come
To tell the wind to stop
To see how deep the sea is
LOW.why: The text says a good surfer looks for the best wave to ride.

wrong.B: The text does not say surfers count waves.
wrong.C: Surfers cannot tell the wind to stop.
wrong.D: Depth matters near the shore, but it is not why surfers watch waves.

LOW.stem: What happens to the bottom of a wave when the water gets less deep?
options: It gets faster
It turns into wind
It lifts the surfer
It slows down
LOW.why: In the text, near the shore the bottom of the wave slows down.

wrong.A: The top of the wave stays fast, but the bottom slows.
wrong.B: A wave does not turn into wind.
wrong.C: The text does not say the bottom lifts the surfer.

LOW.stem: How does the author start the article?
options: With a question
With short actions
With a rule
With a story
LOW.why: The article starts with the short actions Paddle out, Catch a wave, and Stand up.

wrong.A: The first lines are not a question.
wrong.C: The article does not start with a rule.
wrong.D: The article does not start with a story.

MID.stem: What happens once the surfer's speed matches the speed of the wave?
options: The wave stops moving
The surfer falls into the water
The board starts to sink
The wave's slope catches the board
MID.why: The text says that once the speeds match, the slope of the wave catches the board and lets it glide forward.

wrong.A: The wave keeps moving; it does not stop.
wrong.B: The text says the board glides, not that the surfer falls.
wrong.C: The board floats because of buoyancy, so it does not sink.

MID.stem: What does the word glide mean in "lets it glide forward"?
options: Sink slowly
Move smoothly
Stop suddenly
Spin around
MID.why: The text compares gliding to sliding down a hill, which is a smooth movement.

wrong.A: The board floats, so it does not sink.
wrong.C: The board keeps moving forward, not stopping.
wrong.D: The text does not say the board spins.

MID.stem: Why does the author say riding a wave is almost like sliding down a hill?
options: To help readers picture it
To show that surfing is risky
To explain how winds are made
To tell readers to climb hills
MID.why: The comparison helps readers picture how the board slides down the slope of the wave.

wrong.B: The comparison is about how the board moves, not about danger.
wrong.C: Wind is explained in the second paragraph.
wrong.D: The author does not talk about climbing hills.

MID.stem: Why does the base of a wave slow down close to shore?
options: The wind blows harder there
The surfer paddles against it
The sea floor is close to it
The swell gets bigger there
MID.why: In the text, the water gets shallow near the shore and the base of the wave slows because of the sea floor.

wrong.A: The text does not say the wind blows harder near shore.
wrong.B: The surfer does not slow the base of the wave.
wrong.D: A swell is a group of waves, and its size is not the reason.

HIGH.stem: How far does a swell often travel before it reaches the coast?
options: Only a few feet
Often many miles
About one block
Just across a bay
HIGH.why: A swell often travels a long way across deep water before it reaches the coast.

wrong.A: A few feet is far too short for a swell crossing deep water.
wrong.C: One block is not the distance given in the text.
wrong.D: The text says many miles, not a bay.

HIGH.stem: What does the word buoyancy mean in the article?
options: The speed of an oncoming wave
The downward pull of gravity
The sideways push of wind
The upward push of water
HIGH.why: The article defines buoyancy as the upward push of water on an object placed in it.

wrong.A: Wave speed is what the surfer tries to match.
wrong.B: Gravity pulls the board down the wave, which is a different force.
wrong.C: Wind makes the swell but does not float the board.

HIGH.stem: How does wind help form a swell?
options: It cools the surface water
It pulls the water downward
It transfers energy into it
It carries sand to shore
HIGH.why: The article says wind blowing steadily over the ocean transfers energy into the water, forming a swell.

wrong.A: The text does not say wind cools the water.
wrong.B: Wind pushes energy into the water, not down.
wrong.D: Sand is not mentioned in the article.

HIGH.stem: Why does the author say surfing depends on timing as much as strength?
options: Surfers must paddle at the right moment
Surfers need strong legs to lift the board
Waves always break at the same time
A heavy board cannot float
HIGH.why: The surfer must paddle hard at the right moment to match the speed of the wave, which is a matter of timing.

wrong.B: The text does not say surfers lift the board with their legs.
wrong.C: Waves break at different times, so surfers must anticipate them.
wrong.D: The board floats because of buoyancy.
